reconcile.connective: Commentators from Gill to Keil & Delitzsch read Matthew's 'whale' as the same loosely-defined term as Jonah's 'great fish,' not a rival species claim.

discrepancy.connective: Bible critic Dennis McKinsey called this pairing 'the most famous scientific error by Jesus,' arguing that biologically a whale simply is not a fish.

skeptic.name: Dennis McKinsey
skeptic.attribution: Dennis McKinsey, The Encyclopedia of Biblical Errancy (1995)

excerpts.excerpt_text: The great fish (lxx κῆτος, cf. Mat 12:40), which is not more precisely defined, was not a whale, because this is extremely rare in the Mediterranean, and has too small a throat to swallow a man, but a large shark or sea-dog, canis carcharias, or squalus carcharias L., which is very common in the Mediterranean, and has so large a throat, that it can swallow a living man whole.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly ties the LXX Greek kētos (also used by Matthew) to the Hebrew 'great fish,' showing the two texts share one loosely-defined term rather than naming rival species.

excerpts.excerpt_text: The fish, through a mistranslation of , was formerly supposed to be a whale; there, as here, the original means "a great fish." The whale's neck is too narrow to receive a man.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Frames 'whale' as a mistranslation of the same underlying term rendered 'great fish,' and gives the biological reason a literal-whale reading fails.

excerpts.excerpt_text: In Mat 12:40, it is said to be a "whale"; but then that must be understood, not as the proper name of a fish, but as common to all great fishes; otherwise the whale, properly so called, it is said, has not a swallow large enough to take down a man; though some deny this, and assert they are capable of it.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Explicitly reconciles Matthew's 'whale' with Jonah's 'great fish' by reading 'whale' as a generic label for large sea creatures, not a taxonomic claim.

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832), note on Jonah 1:17
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke argues the Hebrew dag gadol could not denote a literal whale and explicitly cross-references his fuller treatment of the same question at Matthew 12:40, keying the harmonization directly to this passage (Haley's 1874 Discrepancies survey does not treat the Jonah fish/whale question, so Clarke is used in its place per the contract's fallback).
